topics.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, screens can be many things: rest, a deep interest, a social world, a buffer against overload. Gaming side by side or watching together can be true togetherness. The honest question isn’t ‘how much screen time?’ but ‘do we each get the attention we need from each other?’
topics.together: Attention is the gift that matters, and screens can steal it or share it. Agree on the times you’re fully present, and enjoy the times you’re happily side by side.
topics.question: When does a screen bring you closer, and when does it pull you apart?
topics.try: Agree on one phone-free half hour each day, and one screen thing you enjoy together.

topics.title: Anger
topics.philosophy: Seneca thought anger was a brief madness and warned against acting on it. Aristotle took a more mixed view: being angry at the right person, for the right reason, in the right way and for the right time can be fitting, but it’s hard to get right. Martha Nussbaum adds that the useful part of anger is the signal that something is wrong; the wish for payback rarely helps.
topics.psychology: Anger often sits on top of other feelings, like hurt, fear or tiredness. Research suggests that venting (ranting, hitting pillows) tends to keep anger going rather than releasing it. Slowing down, naming the feeling and dealing with the problem later work better.
topics.autistic_lens: Many autistic people describe anger that is really overload, or a strong reaction to unfairness. Through an autistic lens, asking ‘what’s too much right now?’ or ‘what feels unfair?’ often gets closer to the root than ‘calm down’. A strong sense of justice is a value, even when it comes out loud.
topics.together: Anger carries a message; let it cool before you deliver it. If anyone feels afraid of someone’s anger, that’s about safety, not communication: please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
topics.question: What is your anger usually trying to protect?
topics.try: Next time you’re angry, finish this sentence before speaking: ‘Underneath this, I feel ___.’

topics.title: Naming what you feel
patterns: \b(don t|do not|can t) (know|name|tell) what i (feel|m feeling)\b
topics.philosophy: Spinoza argued that a passion which rules us loses some of its grip once we understand it clearly. The Stoics, too, thought feelings carry judgments we can examine. Naming a feeling isn’t cold; it’s a way of making friends with what’s inside.
topics.psychology: Lisa Feldman Barrett’s research on emotional granularity suggests that people who can name feelings precisely (‘disappointed’ rather than just ‘bad’) tend to cope better. Matthew Lieberman’s work on ‘affect labeling’ found that putting feelings into words can calm the brain’s alarm response. Interoception, sensing the body’s inner signals, is part of knowing what you feel.
topics.autistic_lens: Many autistic people experience alexithymia, difficulty identifying or naming feelings, and some sense inner body signals differently. Through an autistic lens, it helps to start from the body: ‘my chest is tight and my jaw is clenched’ is real information. Others can help by asking simple, concrete questions instead of ‘how do you feel?’
topics.together: Feelings get easier to handle once they have names, and the body is a good place to start. Be patient with each other: some people find the words fast, and some need time and a map.
topics.question: Where in your body do you notice a feeling before you have a word for it?
topics.try: Three times today, write one body signal and one feeling word that might fit it.

topics.title: Reading your state first
links: WP-02: how full is your battery?
topics.philosophy: Epictetus taught that we are disturbed not by things, but by our judgments about things. A tired, hungry mind makes harsher judgments. Knowing your state first is a Stoic habit: check the lens before trusting the view.
topics.psychology: Stress research shows that the body’s state shapes how we read others: under stress, neutral faces and words can seem hostile. The old HALT check (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) is a simple way to catch this. ‘Read your state first’ and the Battery are this site’s ideas, built on that research.
topics.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, checking your state is often a daily skill: how many spoons, how much sensory load? Many autistic people learned to watch their battery because they had to, and that habit helps everyone. Saying it out loud (‘I’m at twenty per cent today’) helps the other person read your words fairly.
topics.together: Check the lens before you trust the view. Saying your state out loud lets both people adjust, so a tired moment doesn’t turn into a fight about something else.
topics.question: How full is your battery right now, honestly?
topics.try: Before your next hard talk, each give your energy a number from 1 to 10. If either is under 4, pick another time.

topics.title: The same fight again
links: How to stop fighting with your partner
topics.philosophy: The Stoics would ask what is in your control here: not the other person’s nature, but your response and the setup you share. Wittgenstein thought some problems aren’t so much solved as dissolved, once we see them differently. A repeating fight may be a question asked the wrong way.
topics.psychology: Gottman found that many couple conflicts are ‘perpetual’: rooted in lasting differences of personality or need. Happy couples don’t solve them so much as learn to talk about them with humour and kindness. Andrew Christensen and Neil Jacobson’s acceptance-based approach suggests accepting some differences can ease a fight more than trying to change each other.
topics.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, a repeating fight is often a pattern asking to be written down: same trigger, same words, same ending. Many autistic people are skilled at spotting patterns, and that’s a gift here. Map the loop, then change one step on purpose, before the next round.
topics.together: A fight that keeps coming back is usually about a difference to manage, not a contest to win. See the pattern, accept the difference, and change the setup.
topics.question: If your repeating fight were a script, what would the first line be?
topics.try: Write down the last three times this fight happened: what started it, what was said, how it ended. Look for the loop.

topics.title: Fix the setup, not the person
links: The Five Pillars: fix the setup
topics.philosophy: Aristotle said we become just by doing just things: character follows practice. That means changing the practice slowly changes the person. The Stoics would add that you can’t control someone’s character, but you can help shape the setup you share.
topics.psychology: Research on habits shows that cues and surroundings drive much of what we do. Peter Gollwitzer’s ‘implementation intentions’ (‘when X happens, I’ll do Y’) make follow-through more likely. Nagging tends to make people defensive; changing the setup avoids the argument altogether.
topics.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, ‘try harder’ is not a plan. A visual reminder, a fixed time, a clear owner: those are plans. Many autistic and ADHD people rely on outside structure because memory and willpower aren’t reliable for anyone, and that structure helps everyone in the house.
topics.together: When something keeps going wrong, look at the setup before you look at the person. Clear cues and clear owners do more than criticism ever can.
topics.question: What keeps going wrong that you’ve been blaming on character instead of setup?
topics.try: Pick one slipping job and add a cue: a time, a place, an alarm or a note.

topics.title: Foster, adoptive, kinship and stepfamilies
topics.philosophy: Ubuntu holds that a person becomes a person through other people, which fits families built by choice and circumstance as well as by birth. Confucian thought sees family roles as practices you grow into. Care ethics says the work of caring creates real bonds, whatever the paperwork says.
topics.psychology: Attachment research (John Bowlby, Mary Ainsworth and those who followed) shows children need at least one steady, responsive adult, and that this bond can still be built later in childhood. Patricia Papernow’s work on stepfamilies suggests closeness takes years, not months, and that rushing it tends to backfire.
topics.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, a child joining a new home faces a flood of new rules, smells, voices and routines. Saying the house rules out loud, keeping some things from the old home the same, and warning before changes can make a huge difference. Predictability is a way of saying ‘you’re safe here’.
topics.together: Families made by care are real families, and trust grows slowly through steady, predictable care. Say the rules, keep the routines, and give it time.
topics.question: What could help a new member of your family feel safe sooner?
topics.try: Write down five house rules in plain words, for someone who has just arrived.

big_questions.title: What is love?
links: Love languages: a menu, not a label
big_questions.philosophy: Philosophers disagree, which is part of the fun. Plato’s Symposium offers many answers in one evening, from love as longing for what we lack to love as a ladder towards the good. Aristotle saw the best love as wanting good things for someone for their own sake. Erich Fromm and bell hooks both called love a practice, not only a feeling.
big_questions.psychology: Researchers often split love into parts. Robert Sternberg’s triangle names intimacy, passion and commitment. Attachment research describes love as a safe base you can return to. Harry Reis’s work on ‘perceived partner responsiveness’ suggests that feeling understood, valued and cared for sits close to the heart of it.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people describe love very concretely: love is remembering how I take my tea, warning me before plans change, listening to me talk about my favourite thing, letting me be quiet. Through an autistic lens, love is less about grand words and more about reliable, specific care. That’s a definition anyone can use.
big_questions.together: Love may be best understood as what you do, again and again, for someone’s own good, in a way they can actually receive. The feeling matters, and the practice is how it lives.
big_questions.question: What’s one small, specific thing someone does that makes you feel loved?
big_questions.try: Tell someone one specific thing they do that feels like love to you.

big_questions.title: Is fairness always equal?
links: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair
Is the setup working for everyone?
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle said justice treats equals equally and unequals in proportion, which means fair isn’t always the same. Rawls’s difference principle allows unequal shares only when they help those who have least. Marx’s famous slogan, ‘from each according to ability, to each according to needs’, points to need rather than sameness.
big_questions.psychology: Research finds that people use different fairness rules in different settings: equality, equity (by contribution) or need. Close relationships lean towards need. What makes any rule feel fair is often the process: being heard, and having a say.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people care deeply about fairness and consistency, and find it hard when the rules quietly change. Through an autistic lens, the answer is clear: any fair rule can work, as long as it is said out loud, agreed, and applied the same way to everyone.
big_questions.together: Fair can be equal, proportional or by need. The fairest choice is the one both people made with open eyes, and can check again later.
big_questions.question: In your home, which kind of fair are you using: equal, by effort, or by need?
big_questions.try: Name the fairness rule you use for one shared job, and ask whether the other person would choose the same.

big_questions.title: Why do we fight with the people we love?
patterns: \bwhy do i (hurt|snap at) the (ones|people) i love\b
links: How to stop fighting with your partner
Chapter I: why we get out of tune
big_questions.philosophy: The more we care, the more is at stake. The Stoics noticed that strong attachment brings strong reactions, and Buddhist teaching links clinging with suffering. Neither meant we should stop loving; they meant we should notice what we’re holding on to.
big_questions.psychology: Close people share more tasks, more space and more history, so there’s more to disagree about. We also feel safe enough to show our worst moods at home. Attachment research suggests that many fights carry a hidden question underneath: ‘Are you there for me?’
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, many home fights are double empathy problems in miniature: two people following different rules, each sure their own are obvious. Saying ‘here’s the rule I thought we had’ often turns a fight into a puzzle you solve together.
big_questions.together: We fight with the people we love because we’re close enough to collide and care enough to mind. Look for the hidden question and the hidden rule, and the fight often softens.
big_questions.question: What’s the hidden question under your most common fight?
big_questions.try: In your next disagreement, ask: ‘What rule did you think we had?’ Then share yours.

big_questions.title: Can people change?
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle believed character is formed by habit, so change is possible, but slow, and it comes through practice rather than promises. The Buddhist idea of impermanence says nothing about us is fixed. The existentialists went further: we are always, in part, choosing who we are.
big_questions.psychology: James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente’s stages of change describe people moving from not considering change, to thinking about it, preparing, acting and keeping it up, often with slips along the way. Personality research shows traits can shift over a lifetime, especially when people want to change and practise. Lasting change usually comes from inside; pressure from outside rarely does it.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, ‘can they change?’ needs a clearer question: change what, exactly, and how would we know? Some things, like core wiring, aren’t meant to change. Habits and agreements can. Being specific protects both people from impossible hopes.
big_questions.together: People can change their habits, slowly, when they choose to and have a setup that helps. Be clear about which change you mean, and remember some differences are to be accepted, not fixed. Waiting for someone to stop frightening or controlling you is different; that’s a safety question, so please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: What exactly would be different if the change you hope for happened?
big_questions.try: Write the change you hope for as one action you could see, not as a trait.

big_questions.title: What do we owe our family?
links: Supporting family: parents, money home and duty
big_questions.philosophy: Confucius put respect for parents at the root of a good life. Jane English argued that adult children owe their parents what love and friendship call for, not repayment of a debt. Ubuntu suggests we owe each other because we are made by each other. Few philosophers say we owe family our safety or our self.
big_questions.psychology: Research on families suggests duty can bring meaning, and too much of it brings strain. Bowen’s idea of ‘differentiation’ describes staying connected without losing yourself. Healthy families can hold both love and limits.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, ‘family first’ is too vague a rule to live by. It helps to name what you actually give and can give: time, money, care, visits. Many autistic people find that clear, kept promises feel more loving than vague, broken ones.
big_questions.together: We owe family care that grows from real relationship, given in a size we can keep up. Duty never requires accepting fear or harm; if that’s part of it, please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: If you wrote down what you owe your family, what would be on the list, and what wouldn’t?
big_questions.try: Write one family promise you can keep fully, and one you’ve been making but can’t keep.

big_questions.title: Is it selfish to have boundaries?
links: For grown-up children: boundaries with a parent
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle discussed self-love and split it in two: the grasping kind that takes the most for yourself, and the good kind that cares for your own character. Kant thought we have duties to ourselves as well as to others. Caring for yourself can be part of being good to others.
big_questions.psychology: Research on caregivers and burnout suggests that people without limits often end up able to give less, not more, over time. Clear boundaries tend to go with healthier, longer-lasting relationships. Guilt about a boundary is common, and it isn’t proof you did wrong.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people have been told their needs are selfish: needing quiet, needing to leave early, needing plans in writing. Through an autistic lens, a boundary is honest information that lets you keep showing up. Hiding your limits until you collapse helps nobody.
big_questions.together: A boundary is selfish only if it takes from others what they truly need; most boundaries just tell others what you can give. If someone punishes you for having one, that’s worth a closer look: please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: What would you be able to give more freely if your limits were clear?
big_questions.try: Notice one time this week when you say yes but mean no. Practise one honest ‘not today’.

big_questions.title: What makes a good friend?
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle said a true friend wants your good for your own sake, and called a friend ‘another self’. Epicurus counted friendship among the greatest goods of a happy life. Confucius valued friends who are upright, sincere and well-informed, even when their honesty stings.
big_questions.psychology: Studies of friendship point to responsiveness, reliability and shared time. Small, regular contact keeps friendships alive more than big, rare events. Being a good friend also includes letting yourself be helped.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people describe good friends simply: people who say what they mean, accept you as you are, and don’t punish you for missing social rules. Through an autistic lens, a good friend explains instead of withdrawing, and asks instead of assuming.
big_questions.together: A good friend wants your good, tells you the truth kindly, and accepts the shape of you. Say plainly what friendship looks like for you, and ask the same.
big_questions.question: Which friend accepts you most as you are, and have you told them?
big_questions.try: Tell one friend one specific reason you value them.

big_questions.title: Why do small things matter so much?
big_questions.philosophy: Iris Murdoch thought moral life happens mostly in small moments of attention, not in big choices. Confucian ritual says small, everyday courtesies carry respect. Small things are where character lives.
big_questions.psychology: Gottman’s research on bids found that tiny daily responses say a lot about a relationship’s future. Small things also carry meaning: an unwashed cup can stand for ‘my effort doesn’t count’. The peak–end rule shows that brief moments can colour a whole memory.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, small things matter because details matter. Many autistic people notice small changes others miss, and a small broken promise can feel like a broken rule. Taking small things seriously, without turning them into tests, is a way of respecting each other.
big_questions.together: Small things matter because they carry big meanings and they happen every day. Ask what the small thing stands for, and you’ll usually find what really needs to be said.
big_questions.question: What does the small thing that bothers you stand for?
big_questions.try: Next time a little thing stings, finish this sentence: ‘This feels like it means ___.’

big_questions.title: What makes a home?
links: Sharing a room: a roommate agreement
big_questions.philosophy: Gaston Bachelard wrote that a house shelters daydreaming, so home is as much inside us as around us. Heidegger linked dwelling with looking after a place, not just living in it. Ubuntu reminds us that a home is made of people as well as walls.
big_questions.psychology: Research on ‘place attachment’ shows people bond with places that feel safe and familiar. A place feels like home when you can rest, be yourself and predict what will happen. Fair sharing helps; quiet resentment can make even a lovely house feel tense.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, home is the place where you don’t have to mask: the lights are right, the noise is bearable, the routines hold. Building a home around everyone’s senses and needs is one of the deepest kinds of care.
big_questions.together: Home is a place where you can rest, be known and predict what’s coming. Shared fairly and shaped around real needs, almost any space can become one.
big_questions.question: What one change would make your home feel more like home?
big_questions.try: Each name one thing that makes home feel safe to you. Protect it this week.

big_questions.title: Is honesty always kind?
links: WP-09: say it so it lands
big_questions.philosophy: Kant famously held that lying is always wrong, even to spare feelings. Buddhist right speech adds conditions: speech should be true, helpful, kindly meant and well timed. Put together, they suggest: don’t lie, and don’t use the truth as a weapon either.
big_questions.psychology: Research on feedback shows that honest, specific, caring feedback helps people grow, while harsh criticism makes them defensive. In close relationships, many people say they would rather hear a kind truth than a comfortable lie.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people experience honesty as a form of respect: I tell you the truth because I trust you to handle it. Through an autistic lens, ‘brutal’ is the problem, not ‘honest’. Directness with warmth (‘I love you, and I don’t like that shirt’) is one of the clearest gifts there is.
big_questions.together: Honesty is kind when it’s true, needed, gentle and well timed. You don’t have to choose between truth and kindness; you get to choose how you carry the truth.
big_questions.question: Is there something true you’ve been afraid to say kindly?
big_questions.try: Before sharing a hard truth, check three things: is it true, is it helpful, is this the right time?

big_questions.title: Does forgiving mean forgetting?
big_questions.philosophy: Arendt saw forgiveness as freeing both people from being stuck in one act. Martha Nussbaum is wary of forgiveness that is really a demand for grovelling, and prefers a generous love that looks forward. Neither says forgiving means pretending the past didn’t happen.
big_questions.psychology: Researchers separate forgiveness, an inner letting go of payback, from reconciliation, rebuilding trust together. You can do one without the other. Forgiving often helps the forgiver’s own wellbeing, but it can’t be rushed.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people say: I can forgive, but I can’t un-know. Through an autistic lens, that’s honest, not grudging. Forgiveness can sit alongside a clear memory and clear new rules.
big_questions.together: Forgiving means setting down the debt, not erasing the memory, and not necessarily going back. If going back would mean being unsafe, please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: What would you still need to remember, even after you forgive?
big_questions.try: Write: ‘I can forgive ___, and I still need ___.’

big_questions.title: How do we know what someone means?
big_questions.philosophy: Wittgenstein argued that meaning lives in use: we understand words through shared practices. Grice showed how much we imply without saying. In a famous old exchange, Zhuangzi says the fish are happy, and his friend Huizi asks how he could know, since he isn’t a fish. We never fully stand inside another mind.
big_questions.psychology: Research suggests we’re less accurate at reading others than we think, especially over text. The ‘illusion of transparency’ makes us believe our own feelings show more than they do. Asking checks understanding far better than guessing.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, the honest answer is: often we don’t, and that’s fine, because we can ask. The double empathy problem reminds us both sides guess wrong. ‘Did you mean ___?’ isn’t awkward; it’s the most reliable tool we have.
big_questions.together: We know what someone means by asking, checking and learning how they use words, not by guessing harder. Make ‘did you mean...?’ a normal question in your home.
big_questions.question: When did you last guess someone’s meaning instead of asking?
big_questions.try: Use ‘Did you mean ___ or ___?’ three times this week, kindly.

big_questions.title: Why is change so hard?
big_questions.philosophy: Hume said custom guides most of life, so changing a habit means going against our strongest guide. Aristotle saw that good habits take practice, and that it’s easier to start well than to unlearn. Buddhist teaching adds that we cling to what’s familiar, even when it hurts.
big_questions.psychology: Habits run on cues and rewards and don’t need our attention, which is why they’re hard to shift. Change usually involves slips; the stages-of-change model treats a slip as part of the process, not as failure. Small, specific steps beat big resolutions.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people know this in their bones: even a good change can cost a lot of energy. Through an autistic lens, change is easier when it’s planned, explained and taken one piece at a time. That isn’t rigidity; it’s a sensible way for anyone to change.
big_questions.together: Change is hard because habit is powerful and the familiar feels safe. Make it small, specific and planned, and expect a few slips along the way.
big_questions.question: What’s the smallest version of the change you want?
big_questions.try: Write one ‘when X happens, I will do Y’ plan for the change you want.

big_questions.title: What is enough?
big_questions.philosophy: Epicurus thought happiness needs little: friends, freedom and a thoughtful life. The Daoist classic attributed to Laozi says that knowing you have enough is itself a kind of wealth. Seneca warned that whoever always craves more is poor, whatever they own.
big_questions.psychology: Hedonic adaptation means more rarely feels like more for long. Research on perfectionism links ‘never enough’ standards with stress and burnout. Kristin Neff’s research on self-compassion suggests that treating yourself as you’d treat a friend helps people keep going.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, ‘enough’ needs a definition, or it never arrives. Many autistic people find relief in writing it down: ‘Enough cleaning today is the kitchen and one load of washing.’ A clear finish line is a kindness to yourself and to everyone else.
big_questions.together: Enough is a line you can draw on purpose. Name it clearly, honour it when you reach it, and let rest be part of a good day.
big_questions.question: What would ‘enough’ look like for today, in one sentence?
big_questions.try: Write tomorrow’s ‘enough’ list before bed. When it’s done, stop.

big_questions.title: Is it okay to need routines?
big_questions.philosophy: Hume thought custom is how humans get through life at all. Monasteries and many faiths have built whole lives around a daily rule: a set rhythm of work, prayer and rest. Routine has a long and honourable history.
big_questions.psychology: Habits free up attention and lower stress. Research on intolerance of uncertainty shows that some people find unpredictability truly distressing, and that predictability helps them cope. Needing routine isn’t a flaw; it’s information about how you work best.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people say routine is how they stay regulated in a loud, unpredictable world. Through an autistic lens, needing routine is like needing glasses: you work better with it, and there’s no shame in that. The kind thing is to build routines that also leave the other person room to breathe.
big_questions.together: Yes, it’s okay to need routines. Say what yours protect, so others can respect them, and agree together on what to do when life changes the plan.
big_questions.question: Which of your routines would you protect first, and why?
big_questions.try: Tell someone close about one routine you need, and what happens for you when it breaks.

big_questions.title: Who am I, really?
links: Know yourself, then: where your lens came from
big_questions.philosophy: ‘Know yourself’ was carved at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, and Socrates made the question his life’s work. Hume looked inward and found no fixed self, only a bundle of perceptions; Buddhist teaching on non-self says something similar. Ubuntu says the self is made in relationship.
big_questions.psychology: Psychologists such as Dan McAdams describe a ‘narrative identity’: the self as a story we tell, built from memory and shaped by the people around us. Our families, our wiring and our choices each write parts of it.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people describe learning about their wiring as finding a missing piece of themselves. Through an autistic lens, knowing yourself includes knowing your senses, your energy and your way of communicating. It’s practical self-knowledge, the kind you can write on a card.
big_questions.together: The self is partly given, partly chosen and partly made with others. Knowing your own wiring, story and values is a gift to you and to everyone who shares life with you.
big_questions.question: Which part of yourself did you discover only recently?
big_questions.try: Write three lines: ‘I was shaped by ___. I’m wired to ___. I’m choosing to become ___.’

big_questions.title: Is it wrong to want time alone?
links: One wants to talk, one needs space
big_questions.philosophy: Montaigne advised keeping a ‘back room’ of your own. Pascal suggested that much human trouble comes from not being able to sit quietly alone in a room. Arendt thought solitude, being with yourself, is where thinking happens.
big_questions.psychology: Research on introversion and solitude suggests chosen time alone helps many people recharge. Time alone is different from withdrawing in anger: one restores, the other avoids. Often the difference is in how it’s explained.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people need alone time the way others need sleep. Through an autistic lens, the kind way to take it is to say it plainly: ‘I need an hour alone. It’s not about you. I’ll come and find you after.’ Said that way, alone time protects the relationship.
big_questions.together: Wanting time alone isn’t wrong; it’s often how people come back to each other well. Say why, say when you’ll be back, and keep that promise.
big_questions.question: How do you explain your need for time alone, and how does it land?
big_questions.try: Write your ‘time alone’ sentence: what you need, why, and when you’ll return.

big_questions.title: Why do I feel guilty when I rest?
big_questions.philosophy: Josef Pieper argued that leisure is the basis of culture, not a reward for work. Bertrand Russell questioned the belief that work is always a virtue. Many faith traditions command rest, as if they knew people wouldn’t take it otherwise.
big_questions.psychology: Guilt about rest is often driven by ‘should’ rules we learned early. Research links constant busyness with burnout. When the load at home is uneven, the person carrying more often finds rest hardest to take.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, rest is maintenance, like charging a phone. Many autistic people have learned that ignoring the battery leads to shutdown or burnout. Saying ‘I’m resting so I can keep going’ turns guilt into a plan.
big_questions.together: Guilt about rest often comes from an old rule or an uneven load. Check both: rewrite the rule, and share the load so everyone gets to rest.
big_questions.question: Whose voice says you haven’t earned rest yet?
big_questions.try: Take fifteen minutes of rest today, and say out loud: ‘This is part of the work.’

big_questions.title: Can you love someone and still be angry?
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle thought anger can be fitting when it’s about a real wrong and kept in proportion. Martha Nussbaum argues that anger in love works best when it turns into the question of how to make things better. Love and anger aren’t opposites; not caring at all is much further from love.
big_questions.psychology: Most people feel anger towards the people they love most, because those people matter most. What predicts harm isn’t anger itself but how it’s expressed: Gottman found contempt and harsh criticism wound, while a calm complaint about a specific thing can help.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, two feelings can be true at once, and saying both plainly is clearest: ‘I love you. I’m angry that the plan changed without anyone telling me.’ Many autistic people find that naming both stops the other person guessing which one is real.
big_questions.together: Yes, you can love someone and be angry. Say both, and aim the anger at the problem, not the person. If anger ever makes someone afraid, that’s a safety issue: please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: What is your anger asking the person you love to understand?
big_questions.try: Try the two-part sentence: ‘I love you, and I’m angry about ___.’

big_questions.title: What does it mean to really listen?
big_questions.philosophy: Simone Weil thought that being able to give real attention to someone who is suffering is very rare, and very precious. Buber’s I–Thou describes meeting a person fully instead of using them. Real listening is a moral act, not just a skill.
big_questions.psychology: Carl Rogers described empathic listening as entering another person’s world without judging it. Research on active listening suggests reflecting back what you heard helps people feel understood. Listening to fix is different from listening to understand.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people listen without eye contact, or while stimming or doodling, and get told they aren’t listening. Through an autistic lens, real listening is about attention, not performance. Asking ‘do you want ideas, or just someone to hear this?’ helps everyone.
big_questions.together: To really listen is to give full attention to someone’s world without rushing to fix it. Ask what kind of listening they want, and let them show attention in their own way too.
big_questions.question: Who really listens to you, and what do they do?
big_questions.try: Next time someone shares something, ask: ‘Do you want help, or do you want me to listen?’

big_questions.title: Why does being misunderstood hurt so much?
big_questions.philosophy: Hegel, and Axel Honneth after him, argued that we become ourselves through being recognised by others, so being misread can feel like being erased. Wittgenstein suggested we understand each other within shared forms of life; where those differ, misunderstanding is natural, not anyone’s fault.
big_questions.psychology: Research on perceived partner responsiveness finds that feeling understood is central to closeness. Being misunderstood again and again tends to go with loneliness. Naive realism makes each side sure the other is the one misreading.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people know this hurt well, after years of being misread. The double empathy problem gives a kinder frame: misunderstanding runs both ways, and nobody is the only cause. Through an autistic lens, the fix is translation, not blame: ‘Here’s what I meant. What did you hear?’
big_questions.together: Being misunderstood hurts because we need recognition, and it often comes from different wiring, not bad intent. Translate both ways, patiently, and say what you meant in plain words.
big_questions.question: What do you most wish people understood about you?
big_questions.try: Write one line for others: ‘When I ___, it usually means ___.’ Share it with someone.

big_questions.title: What do we owe each other at home?
links: Chapter II: is the split working?
big_questions.philosophy: Arendt saw promises as islands of certainty in an uncertain future. Kant’s respect, de Beauvoir’s reciprocity and care ethics’ attention all suggest we owe each other honesty, fairness and care. Susan Moller Okin insisted that justice doesn’t stop at the front door.
big_questions.psychology: Research on equity, responsiveness and trust suggests people feel secure when effort is shared, needs are noticed and promises are kept. Small, repeated reliability builds trust more than grand gestures.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, what we owe each other should be written plainly enough to check: who does what, how we tell each other things, what we do when we disagree. Many autistic people find that clear agreements make love feel safe, not less romantic.
big_questions.together: At home we owe each other fairness, honesty, attention and kept promises. Say them out loud, write the practical ones down, and check them now and then.
big_questions.question: What’s one promise your household has never said out loud?
big_questions.try: Write three ‘we will’ sentences for your home and read them together.

big_questions.title: Is it okay to be different?
big_questions.philosophy: John Stuart Mill argued that people should be free to live by their own lights, as long as they don’t harm others, and that everyone gains from different ‘experiments in living’. Ubuntu holds that each person’s humanity is bound up with everyone else’s, differences included.
big_questions.psychology: Neurodiversity research and personality science both show that human minds vary widely. Research on belonging suggests feeling accepted matters a great deal for wellbeing, and that hiding differences costs energy. Being different is not the same as being wrong.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people spent years being told they were ‘too much’ or ‘not enough’. Through an autistic lens, difference is just difference: another way of sensing, thinking and loving. Spreading acceptance starts with accepting yourself.
big_questions.together: Yes, it’s okay to be different. Difference makes life richer, and acceptance, of yourself and of others, is the ground every fair relationship grows from.
big_questions.question: What difference in you would you like to stop apologising for?
big_questions.try: Write one sentence about a difference of yours that begins: ‘I’m glad I ___.’

big_questions.title: What does acceptance mean?
big_questions.philosophy: The Stoics taught acceptance of what we can’t control, alongside action on what we can. Buddhist teaching invites us to meet what is, without clinging. Kant’s idea of dignity says a person’s worth doesn’t depend on their usefulness or their agreeing with us.
big_questions.psychology: Carl Rogers described ‘unconditional positive regard’: valuing a person without having to approve of everything they do. Andrew Christensen and Neil Jacobson’s acceptance-based couple therapy found that accepting some differences can ease conflict more than trying to change them. Acceptance is not giving up on fairness.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, acceptance means letting people be the shape they are: the stimmer, the planner, the talker, the quiet one. Many autistic people say being accepted feels like finally being able to breathe. It doesn’t mean putting up with unfairness; it means not treating a difference as a defect.
big_questions.together: Acceptance means valuing who someone is while still being honest about what you need: accept the person, and talk about the setup. Acceptance never means accepting fear or harm; if that’s the question, please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html).
big_questions.question: What would change if you accepted one difference instead of trying to fix it?
big_questions.try: Name one difference between you and someone close that you could stop arguing with, and one setup you could talk about instead.

big_questions.title: Why do we take people for granted?
big_questions.philosophy: Heraclitus and the Buddhists remind us that everything changes, yet we act as if the people we love will always be there. The Stoics practised imagining loss, not to be gloomy, but to feel grateful now. Murdoch would call taking someone for granted a failure of attention.
big_questions.psychology: Hedonic adaptation makes the good things in life fade into the background. Research on gratitude (Sara Algoe and others) suggests that noticing and naming what others do renews appreciation on both sides.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, taking someone for granted is often a routine that stopped being noticed, not a lack of love. Many autistic people would suggest a practical fix: build the noticing into the routine. ‘Every Friday, we each name one thing the other did.’
big_questions.together: We take people for granted because our minds get used to good things. Notice on purpose, say thanks specifically, and make that part of your routine.
big_questions.question: Who in your life have you stopped noticing?
big_questions.try: Tonight, name one specific thing someone close did this week that you hadn’t mentioned.

big_questions.title: What makes life meaningful?
big_questions.philosophy: Aristotle thought a good life (eudaimonia) comes from using our best capacities, with friends, over a whole life. Susan Wolf argues that meaning arises when ‘subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness’: caring about something that is worth caring about. Ubuntu finds meaning in being with and for others.
big_questions.psychology: Research on meaning in life (Michael Steger and others) links it with having purpose, a sense that life hangs together, and a feeling that it matters. Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist, wrote that meaning can be found in work, in love, and in the attitude we take to suffering. Close relationships are among the most common sources of meaning people name.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people find deep meaning in their special interests, in justice, and in a few close bonds. Through an autistic lens, meaning doesn’t have to be grand or social. Loving one subject deeply, or caring for one person well, can be a full and meaningful life.
big_questions.together: Meaning grows where real care meets something worth caring about, often in ordinary days with the people we share life with. Small, fair, kind acts aren’t a distraction from meaning; they’re a big part of it.
big_questions.question: What do you care about that you’d still care about if nobody ever noticed?
big_questions.try: Write down one thing you did this week that mattered to someone, however small.

big_questions.title: How do I know if a relationship is worth working on?
patterns: \bhow do i know if (it|this|a relationship|my relationship) is worth\b
big_questions.philosophy: De Beauvoir thought love is real when both people stay free and help each other grow. Aristotle’s test for friendship, wanting each other’s good, works here too. No philosopher worth reading says you must endure fear to prove your love.
big_questions.psychology: Caryl Rusbult’s investment model explains why people stay: how satisfied they are, what their alternatives look like, and what they’ve already invested. Staying because of investment alone can keep people in unhappy places. Gottman’s research suggests contempt is one of the strongest warning signs, while repair and kindness are hopeful ones.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, it helps to ask several concrete questions instead of one huge one: Do I feel safe? Can I be myself here? Are we both trying? Is the load fair? Many autistic people find a written list of specifics clearer than a fog of feelings.
big_questions.together: A relationship is worth working on when both people are safe, both are trying, and both can be themselves. If fear or control is part of it, please start with the “Not safe at home?” page (/safety.html); working harder is not the answer to being unsafe.
big_questions.question: Do you feel safe, free and seen in this relationship, most of the time?
big_questions.try: Write four lines: ‘I feel safe when... I can be myself when... We both try when... It’s fair when...’

big_questions.title: Is it weak to need people?
links: When one of you is ill or disabled
big_questions.philosophy: Alasdair MacIntyre argued that dependence is part of every human life, so the virtues include receiving help well, not only giving it. Ubuntu says we become persons through others. Aristotle thought even the happiest person needs friends.
big_questions.psychology: Attachment research describes what some call ‘effective dependence’: people who can lean on others when needed tend to be more confident, not less. Social support is linked with better health and resilience. Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people were pushed to be ‘independent’ in ways that meant struggling alone. Through an autistic lens, needing support is like using a ramp: it’s how you get where you’re going. Saying exactly what help you need makes it easier for others to give it.
big_questions.together: Needing people is part of being human, and leaning well is a strength. Ask clearly for the help you need, and let yourself receive it.
big_questions.question: What help would you ask for if you were sure nobody would think less of you?
big_questions.try: Ask one person for one specific, small piece of help this week.

big_questions.title: What is kindness?
big_questions.philosophy: Confucius’s ren is often translated as humaneness: caring for others as people like yourself. Buddhist metta, loving-kindness, wishes others well without conditions. Kant would add that kindness should respect the other person’s own choices, not just do what we think is good for them.
big_questions.psychology: Research on kindness suggests small acts lift wellbeing for both the giver and the receiver. Elizabeth Dunn’s studies found that spending money on others tends to make people happier than spending it on themselves. Kindness that fits what the other person wants lands better than kindness we assume they want.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Many autistic people show kindness practically and honestly: fixing a problem, sharing useful information, telling the truth gently. Through an autistic lens, kindness doesn’t have to be smiley or chatty to be real. ‘What would actually help?’ is the kindest question.
big_questions.together: Kindness is caring for someone’s good in a way that respects who they are. The best kindness is asked about, not guessed.
big_questions.question: What’s the kindest thing anyone has done for you, and why did it land?
big_questions.try: Ask someone ‘What would actually help today?’ and do that one thing.

big_questions.title: Why do we keep score?
links: Stories from philosophy: the ethics of a ledger
big_questions.philosophy: Adam Smith, before he wrote about markets, wrote about moral sentiments, including our deep wish to be seen fairly by others. Kant would warn against reducing a person to a balance sheet. Score-keeping is often a fairness instinct with nowhere else to go.
big_questions.psychology: Clark and Mills’s work suggests that people in close relationships tend to track who gives what more closely when the relationship feels less communal, less like ‘we look after each other’. Ross and Sicoly showed we each remember our own efforts more easily. So keeping score is often a sign of hidden unfairness or unseen work, not pettiness.
big_questions.autistic_lens: Through an autistic lens, score-keeping is often a symptom of rules nobody said out loud. If the split were agreed and visible, the tally in your head could stop. Many autistic people would say: write it down once, together, so neither of us has to carry it around.
big_questions.together: We keep score when we feel unseen or the split feels unfair. Put the whole load on one shared page, agree the rules, and the scoreboard in your head can rest.
big_questions.question: What is your score-keeping trying to tell you?
big_questions.try: Write down what you’ve been counting. Then ask: what rule would let me stop counting?
